# The two opposite adjacent-centroid partitions do not select a quarter-depth point

This is an exact counterexample to a particular deterministic selector, not to the mixed-integer Grünbaum conjecture. It already has `n=d=1` and four equal positive interval fibers.

## 1. Actual body, measure, and selector

Let
\[
 C=[-1,2]\times[0,1],\qquad
 S=\{-1,0,1,2\}\times[0,1].
\]
This is an ambient convex body, and its mixed measure is the sum of ordinary interval lengths. In particular `q=d=1`, its total mass is `M=4`, and its true mixed centroid is `(1/2,1/2)`.

The proposed selector writes the base mean as `k+theta`, here `k=0`, `theta=1/2`. It takes the two exposed endpoints of the dominated-source moment interval
\[
 \mathcal M_2(1)=\left\{\frac12\int x f\,d\mu:
 0\le f\le1,\quad\int f\,d\mu=2,\quad\int zf\,d\mu=2\right\},
\]
and also the centroids of their complementary sources, whose base is zero. These are precisely the centroids from the two opposite prescribed continuous normals in the adjacent-integer-centroid partition theorem.

We prove that all four selected points have normalized depth at most `9/40<1/4`.

## 2. The two exposed sources are unique actual convex caps

Consider
\[
 H_+=\{x+z/5\ge3/5\}.
\]
At indices `(-1,0,1,2)` its retained interval lengths are
\[
 (1/5,2/5,3/5,4/5).
\]
Their sum is two and their base first moment is
\[
 -1/5+3/5+8/5=2.
\]
The continuous first moment of its source is
\[
 \sum_z\left(m_z-\frac12m_z^2\right)
 =2-\frac12\frac{1+4+9+16}{25}=\frac75.
\]
Its full centroid is therefore `(1,7/10)`.

This is the unique source maximizing the continuous first moment under the two source constraints. Indeed put `L=x+z/5-3/5`. For any feasible `f`,
\[
 \int L(1_{H_+}-f)\,d\mu\ge0
\]
pointwise: on `L>0` the factor `1-f` is nonnegative; on `L<0` the factor `-f` is nonpositive. The mass and base-moment constraints cancel the affine-in-base part, leaving
\[
 \int x f\,d\mu\le\int_{H_+}x\,d\mu.
\]
Equality requires `f=1_{H_+}` almost everywhere, because the level line `L=0` has zero length in each of the four fibers.

Reflection `x ->1-x` preserves the original measure and the two source constraints. Consequently the unique minimizing source is
\[
 H_- =\{x-z/5\le2/5\},
\]
whose retained lengths are the same and whose centroid is `(1,3/10)`. Thus
\[
 \mathcal M_2(1)=[3/10,7/10].
\]
The original continuous first moment is two. Complementing either mass-two source consequently sends its continuous centroid `y` to `1-y`, at base zero. The four candidates are exactly
\[
 \boxed{(1,7/10),\ (0,3/10),\ (1,3/10),\ (0,7/10).}
\]
The two pairs arise from actual complementary convex caps of `C`. Their overlap lies on a nonvertical line and has zero mixed measure. Thus no fractional-source or unattained-support issue is involved.

## 3. Every candidate fails the quarter-depth bound

At `p=(1,7/10)`, take the closed ambient cap
\[
 H=\{x+(3/10)z\ge1\}.
\]
It contains `p` on its boundary. Its retained lengths at `(-1,0,1,2)` are respectively
\[
 0,\quad0,\quad3/10,\quad3/5.
\]
The zero at base zero includes the endpoint `(0,1)`, but this has zero mixed measure. Hence
\[
 \mu(S\cap H)=9/10<1=M/4,
 \qquad \operatorname{depth}_S(p)\le\frac9{40}<\frac14.
\]
The measure-preserving affine reflections `x ->1-x` and `z ->1-z` preserve `S`, carry ambient closed halfspaces to ambient closed halfspaces, and send `p` to the other three candidates. Therefore every candidate has the same strict failure. The absolute mass deficit is `1/10`, and the normalized deficit is `1/40`.

For comparison, `(1,1/2)` has depth exactly `3/8`. The three-fiber subproduct `{0,1,2} x [0,1]` is centrally symmetric about this point and has mixed mass three. Every containing closed halfspace therefore has mass at least `3/2`. The cap `x+z/2>=1` attains that mass in the full source, with lengths `(0,0,1/2,1)`. This demonstrates explicitly that the proposed selector fails while the original body has a point exceeding the OC guarantee.

## 4. Scope

The example refutes taking the four centroids of the two opposite prescribed-normal adjacent-integer partitions, even when all four original fibers are equal intervals. It does not refute the existence or uniqueness assertions of the partition theorem. It also does not refute choosing some other point of either moment interval, optimizing actual depth over those intervals, or allowing partitions with different continuous normals in dimension greater than one. In dimension one, however, the prescribed nonzero continuous normals have only the two orientations already tested here.
